progressionInfo.name: ii-IV-V Progression
progressionInfo.subtitle: A powerful pre-dominant chain that builds stepwise tension from the minor ii through the subdominant IV to the dominant V. A signature sound in country turnarounds, Nashville songwriting, and bridge sections that creates an irresistible pull back to the tonic.

properties.label: ii (Pre-Dominant)
properties.value: Minor quality chord that initiates motion away from tonic

properties.label: IV (Subdominant)
properties.value: Stepwise rise from ii creates smooth voice leading and builds energy

properties.label: V (Dominant)
properties.value: Strong ascending arrival on the dominant demands resolution to I

properties.label: Stepwise Bass Motion
properties.value: Root movement rises by thirds (ii→IV) then by a whole step (IV→V)

properties.label: Harmonic Momentum
properties.value: All three chords are 'away from home,' creating a powerful desire to resolve to I

chordDiagrams.title: ii-IV-V in C Major
chordDiagrams.description: Open position chords in the key of C:
practiceNotes: The Dm to F transition shares the note F as a common tone
F to G is a strong whole-step bass rise that builds energy
After G, let the progression resolve to C to hear the full turnaround
Try accenting beat 1 of the G chord to emphasize the dominant arrival

advancedApplications.title: Country Turnaround Variations
advancedApplications.description: Extend the ii-IV-V with classic country techniques:
items: Add a walkup bass line: D-E-F-F#-G over the progression
Use a hammer-on from Dm to full F barre for rhythmic drive
Swap V for V7 (G7 in C) to add extra tension before the turnaround
Double the V chord duration for a dramatic half-time resolution
Play the ii as a sus2 (Dsus2) for an open, airy country sound

advancedApplications.title: Seventh Chord Enrichment
advancedApplications.description: Add seventh voicings for fuller harmonic color:
items: ii7: Dm7 (D-F-A-C) adds the key's tonic note as the 7th
IVmaj7: Fmaj7 (F-A-C-E) creates a lush, warm subdominant
V7: G7 (G-B-D-F) provides the classic dominant seventh pull
Chain: Dm7 - Fmaj7 - G7 gives a sophisticated Nashville sound
Try Am7 - Cmaj7 - D7 in the key of G for a folk-country blend

advancedApplications.title: Key Transposition Guide
items: Key of C: Dm - F - G (all open chords, easiest key)
Key of G: Am - C - D (popular for country and folk)
Key of D: Em - G - A (bright, open string resonance)
Key of A: Bm - D - E (requires Bm barre chord)
Key of E: F#m - A - B (common in country-rock)

examples.title: Country Turnarounds
examples.description: The ii-IV-V is a staple ending phrase in country music
examples.detail: Used in the last two bars before repeating a verse or returning to the I chord

examples.title: "Wagon Wheel" Style Progressions
examples.description: The pre-dominant chain creates forward motion in folk-country anthems
examples.detail: Often precedes the big I chord arrival in sing-along choruses

examples.title: Hank Williams Style
examples.description: Classic honky-tonk turnarounds lean on the ii-IV-V movement
examples.detail: Frequently paired with a walking bass line to outline each chord change

examples.title: Nashville Songwriting
examples.description: Modern Nashville writers use ii-IV-V as a bridge or pre-chorus device
examples.detail: Creates emotional lift by stacking non-tonic chords before the chorus payoff

examples.title: Pop-Country Crossover
examples.description: Acts as a tension ramp in pop-country arrangements
examples.detail: Taylor Swift, Keith Urban, and similar artists use this chain for energy builds

examples.title: Southern Rock & Americana
examples.description: Allman Brothers and Lynyrd Skynyrd-style extended jams
examples.detail: The stepwise climb from ii to V provides a springboard for improvisation

practiceCategories.title: Chord Transitions
items: Play Dm - F - G - C at 60 BPM, one strum per beat
Focus on keeping the F note (1st fret, high E) ringing through the Dm-to-F change
Practice the F-to-G shift as a single quick motion
Add a bass walkup (D-E-F-G) under the chord changes
Reverse the progression (G - F - Dm) to internalize the sound both ways

practiceCategories.title: Strumming & Rhythm
items: Use a steady down-down-up-up-down-up country strum pattern
Accent beats 2 and 4 for an authentic country backbeat feel
Try boom-chicka (bass note then chord) on each chord
Increase tempo from 80 to 120 BPM in 10 BPM increments
Experiment with a shuffle feel (swung eighth notes) on the ii-IV-V

practiceCategories.title: Ear Training & Application
items: Sing the bass notes (D-F-G) while playing to internalize the root motion
Listen for the ii-IV-V in country radio songs and identify the turnaround
Transpose the pattern to G major (Am - C - D) and compare the sound
Record yourself playing ii-IV-V and improvise a melody over the loop
Practice resolving to I with different rhythmic feels (half note, whole note, fermata)

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 1: Basic ii-IV-V Turnaround in C
notatedExercises.description: Play the fundamental turnaround using open position triads. Hold each chord for a full bar and listen for the stepwise energy build.
practiceNotes: Hold each chord for 4 beats with a steady downstroke
Listen for the rising bass motion: D to F to G
Resolve to C major on the final bar to complete the turnaround
Keep your fretting hand relaxed during transitions

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 2: Seventh Chord Country Chain
notatedExercises.description: Enrich the turnaround with seventh chords for a more sophisticated Nashville sound. Dm7 - Fmaj7 - G7 resolving to C.
practiceNotes: Notice how the 7th of each chord creates a leading tone to the next root
The C in Dm7 is shared with the following Fmaj7 (common tone)
G7 contains the tritone B-F which resolves strongly to C-E
Use this voicing in verse endings and turnarounds

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 3: Walking Bass Turnaround
notatedExercises.description: Combine the ii-IV-V chords with a country walking bass line. Play the bass note on beats 1 and 3, and strum the chord on beats 2 and 4.
practiceNotes: Alternate between the bass note (thumb) and chord strum (fingers)
Walk from D up through E to F on the Dm-to-F transition
Walk from F through F# to G on the IV-to-V transition
This technique is the foundation of Travis picking in country guitar

sections.title: Bass Line Analysis in C Major
items: ii (D): 2nd degree of C major, the first step away from tonic
IV (F): 4th degree, a minor 3rd above the ii root
V (G): 5th degree, a whole step above IV
The rising root line D-F-G creates increasing harmonic tension
Resolving to I (C) completes the cycle with a descending 5th

sections.title: Why the ii Chord Works Here
items: Dm shares two notes with F major: D is the 6th of F, A is the 3rd of F (but F is shared too: F-A common in both)
The minor quality of ii provides contrast against the major IV and V
ii acts as a 'softer' pre-dominant compared to starting directly on IV
In country music, the ii adds a wistful quality before the IV-V power lift

sections.title: Chord Tone Connections
items: Dm to F: D→C (step down), F→F (common tone), A→A (common tone)
F to G: F→G (step up), A→B (step up), C→D (step up)
Two common tones in the ii-IV change make it exceptionally smooth
Parallel stepwise motion in IV-V creates strong forward drive

sections.title: Compatible Scales for Soloing
items: C major scale (C-D-E-F-G-A-B) works over the entire progression
D Dorian (D-E-F-G-A-B-C) highlights the ii chord flavor
C major pentatonic (C-D-E-G-A) is safe and consonant throughout
G Mixolydian (G-A-B-C-D-E-F) adds a country sound over the V chord
